about.title: Predictive processing and the controlled hallucination
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are four ideas (guessing and checking, the controlled hallucination, the body and self, the critics). Each is taught slowly with a check question, so the class fits the usual length.

say.text: Welcome to class 7. Today's big idea is that your brain may work by guessing, then checking its guesses.

show.text: Predictive processing: the brain as a guessing machine

say.text: We will go in four steps: how guessing works, why perception is called a 'controlled hallucination', what this says about body and self, and then two criticisms.

show.text:
1. Guess and check
2. Controlled hallucination
3. Body, emotion and self
4. Two criticisms

say.text: Step one. In this theory, a prediction is the brain's best guess about what is causing the signals reaching your senses.

show.text: Prediction = a best guess

say.text: The brain compares each guess with the incoming signal. The leftover difference is called a prediction error.

show.text: Prediction error = guess minus signal

say.text: Here is an everyday example. You don't notice your clothes on your skin, because the brain already expects that feeling. If something unexpected touches you, the error is big, and you notice.

show.text: A person sitting calmly, then startled by a sudden tap on the arm

ask.q: In predictive processing, what is mainly passed up from the senses to higher levels of the brain?
ask.right: The mismatch between the guess and the signal (the prediction error)
wrong: A full copy of everything the senses pick up
Only the things you already expected
Only your memories
ask.why: In this theory the brain already has a guess, so what is worth sending up is the part the guess got wrong.

say.text: This flips the usual picture. We tend to think the senses send a picture up to the brain. Here, guesses flow down and errors flow up.

show.text:
Everyday view: senses send the picture UP.
Predictive view: guesses flow DOWN, errors flow UP.

say.text: What does the brain do with errors? It updates its model, so the next guess is better. It can also act, so the world matches the guess. Seth calls that second route active inference.

show.text:
Guess
Compare with the signal
Error found: update the guess, or act to change the signal

ask.q: A guess keeps failing to match the signals. What does the theory say the brain does?
ask.right: It updates its model so the next guess fits better
wrong: It ignores the signals for good
It stops making guesses
It switches off the senses
ask.why: The whole system works by shrinking errors and updating its models when guesses fail.

say.text: Step two. Let's see the guess win over the evidence. Picture a face mask, turned so you look into its hollow inside.

show.text: The hollow inside of a face mask, which still looks like a normal face bulging towards you

say.text: It still looks like a bulging face. Researchers read this as top-down knowledge: you have seen countless bulging faces, so your brain's expectation beats the real shape.

show.text: Expectation can beat the evidence

ask.q: Why does a hollow mask usually look like a bulging face?
ask.right: The brain's strong expectation that faces bulge outward overrides the evidence
wrong: The mask is secretly bulging
The eyes cannot see shapes at all
The mask is lit from behind
ask.why: The illusion is described as a knowledge-based, top-down effect that favours the familiar convex face over the true hollow shape.

say.text: Now we can name the idea. Seth calls perception a controlled hallucination. It is a hallucination in the sense that it is generated from the inside out.

show.text: Controlled hallucination

say.text: And it is controlled because the world keeps correcting it with useful errors.

show.text: perception is a controlled hallucination (Anil Seth's slogan)

ask.q: In the phrase 'controlled hallucination', what does 'controlled' point to?
ask.right: The world's error signals keep the brain's guesses tied to reality
wrong: You can steer your perception by willpower
It only happens during illness
The guesses are random
ask.why: The brain builds the experience, and the world corrects it through prediction errors.

say.text: Notice what this does not say. It does not say the world is unreal. It says there is no bright line between hallucination and ordinary perception. Ordinary perception uses the same machinery, held in check.

show.text:
The world is real
Experience is built by the brain
The world checks the build

say.text: Seth suggests psychedelic experiences are hallucinations that have become uncontrolled. The same guessing machinery runs, with less holding it in check.

show.text: Controlled becomes uncontrolled

say.text: Researchers also use this idea to study psychosis, such as hearing voices. Please remember these are research ideas, not a verdict on any person.

show.text:
Research summaries link hallucinations to perception tilting toward prior beliefs
Hallucinations and delusions may involve different changes
The picture is not simple

ask.q: What does the psychosis review say about hallucinations and delusions?
ask.right: They may relate to distinct changes in predictive coding, even though they often occur together
wrong: One single fault explains both
They have nothing to do with prediction
They are always caused by the same thing
ask.why: The reviewers point out that the two may involve different alterations, which is one challenge for a simple account.

say.text: Step three: the body. Interoception is the brain's sense of the inside of the body. Think of hunger or a pounding heart.

show.text: Interoception = sensing the body from inside

say.text: Seth and Critchley's proposal: the brain also guesses about these inner signals, and an emotion is its best guess about what is causing them.

show.text: Emotion = a best guess about inner body signals

ask.q: On this proposal, what is an emotion?
ask.right: The brain's best guess about the causes of signals from the body
wrong: A direct readout of the body with no guessing
A thought with nothing to do with the body
A guess about what other people are thinking
ask.why: Emotions are described as states built from top-down predictions and bottom-up prediction errors about the body's inner signals.

say.text: Now the famous phrase: beast machine. The philosopher Descartes held that animals were unfeeling machines, like clockwork.

show.text: Beast machine

say.text: Seth turns it around. He suggests our sense of self arises because we are living animal bodies, not in spite of it.

show.text: Selfhood may arise because we are 'beast machines', not despite it (Seth and Friston, 2016)

say.text: What are the body guesses for? Seth says they are control-oriented: they help keep vital body conditions in a safe range, rather than build a perfect picture.

show.text:
Aim: keep the body in balance
Not: a perfect internal picture

say.text: The self is not one thing. It runs from simply being a body, up to reflective self-awareness and the social self. Seth and Tsakiris suggest these all rest on those body-regulating guesses.

show.text: Being a body, then reflective self-awareness, then the social self

say.text: A test case is the rubber hand illusion. Your real hand is hidden. A fake hand is in view. Both are stroked at the same moment.

show.text: A hidden real hand and a visible rubber hand, both stroked with paintbrushes at the same time

say.text: Many people then feel the fake hand is their own. One prediction-based account says the brain predicts when touch should arrive, and the matching timing confirms it.

show.text: Matching timing, so 'that hand is mine'

ask.q: What is done to make the rubber hand illusion work?
ask.right: The hidden real hand and the visible rubber hand are stroked at the same time
wrong: Only the rubber hand is stroked, once
The real hand is shown and the rubber hand is hidden
Nothing is touched at all
ask.why: The synchronised stroking is what makes the fake hand feel like part of the body.

say.text: So here is the best case. One idea covers illusions, hallucinations and the sense of a body self. Supporters say that unifying power is the reason to take it seriously.

show.text:
Illusions: the hollow mask
Mental illness and hallucination: research under way
The self: the rubber hand and the beast machine

say.text: Step four: criticisms. First, is it too broad to test? A good theory should be able to be proven wrong. Critics say predictive processing is so flexible that it may fit any result.

show.text: Criticism 1: too broad to test?

say.text: One version of the worry is that for any behaviour you can find some set of priors that fits. Defenders reply that some results would count against it.

show.text:
Critics: flexible enough to fit anything.
Defenders: some data patterns would count against it, though adjusting precision complicates this.

ask.q: Why do critics worry predictive processing may be too broad to test?
ask.right: Because adjusting its guesses and their reliability can make it fit almost any result
wrong: Because experiments have already proved it false
Because it only applies to vision
Because nobody has ever measured the brain
ask.why: The concern is flexibility. Defenders reply that some patterns of data would still count against it.

say.text: Second criticism: the hard problem. Easy problems are about how the brain does its jobs. The hard problem asks why any of it is felt at all.

show.text:
Easy problems: how the brain works.
Hard problem: why there is any experience.

say.text: Prediction explains a lot about what we perceive. Does it explain why there is experience at all, or only the easy problems?

show.text: Criticism 2: only the easy problems?

say.text: Seth's reply is the real problem: use brain and body mechanisms to explain, predict and control features of experience. He hopes this dissolves the hard problem rather than solving it.

show.text:
Explain
Predict
Control
...the properties of conscious experience

say.text: Seth accepts that science is not well placed to answer the metaphysical question of why consciousness is in the universe at all. One critic says that means he is avoiding the hard problem.

show.text:
Seth: map experience to mechanisms; the big mystery may shrink.
Critic: that sidesteps the hard problem.

ask.q: What does the 'real problem' approach try to do?
ask.right: Explain, predict and control the features of experience using brain and body mechanisms
wrong: Prove that consciousness does not exist
Answer once and for all why anything is felt
Replace science with philosophy
ask.why: It aims to make progress on the features of experience, hoping the deeper mystery shrinks as the links get closer. Critics say it leaves that mystery open.

say.text: To sum up: the brain guesses and corrects, perception is a controlled hallucination, emotion and self may come from guesses about the body, and there are two big criticisms.

show.text:
Guess and correct
Controlled hallucination
Body, emotion, self
Criticisms: too broad to test? only the easy problems?

ask.q: Which pair names the two criticisms from this class?
ask.right: It may be too broad to test, and it may explain only the 'easy' problems, not why there is experience
wrong: It ignores the body, and it denies emotions exist
It cannot explain any illusions, and it has been proven false
It is too narrow for mental illness, and it is too old
ask.why: Those two are the objections we covered: the worry about testability, and the question of the hard problem.

say.text: Next class, we look at strange loops and the self: how a mind might come to see itself.

show.text: Next: Class 8, Strange loops and the self

notes.topic: the real problem versus the hard problem

other_side.claim: Predictive processing is a testable scientific theory.
other_side.other_view: Critics say it is flexible enough to fit nearly any result. Defenders argue some data patterns would count against it, though adjusting precision complicates this.

other_side.claim: Predictive processing helps with the hard problem of consciousness.
other_side.other_view: Seth aims to dissolve the hard problem and accepts that science is not well placed to address the metaphysical question. One critic says this sidesteps it.

other_side.claim: Experience is fixed by top-down predictions rather than by incoming sensory signals.
other_side.other_view: One reviewer of Seth's book found it unclear why the link to Bayesian inference supports this claim about perceptual content.

other_side.claim: Predictive processing gives a unified account of mental illness.
other_side.other_view: Reviewers note that hallucinations and delusions may involve different changes. A critical review argues that if conditions can come from accurate and inaccurate models alike, the theory's testability is weakened.
